# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

whys.g1: Eleanor's demo walk and my borrowed matinee pair are the same thing -- try it in the real setting before buying -- and 'Try a borrowed pair first' says that plainly, while Ruth's answer about catching audience questions in a big hall is a wish for what it should do, not a trial step, so it rightly sits on its own.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and nothing like that was put in a group.

founder.order_why: The flow runs context, problem, solution and launch sensibly, but the recency screen (4) sits between two screens with the same context heading (3 and 5), so the context step feels split in half.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the identical question 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks about price or who pays. AirCaps is $599 glasses plus an optional $20/month Pro plan, HSA/FSA eligible, and paid for by the wearer, so the flow should ask the price, what people spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and who decides and pays. The pilot screen (19) does not cover the real commitment step either: ordering a pair with 15-day free returns.

PRIMARY.order_why: "What steps did it take?" comes after the phone question inside the idea part, but it reads like a follow-up to losing track of the conversation and belongs right after screen 2, before the idea card.
PRIMARY.missing: What I already do when I lose track, like lip-reading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app on my phone, or bringing an interpreter. Also where the conversation was and how noisy it was (a restaurant, work, the theatre lobby), and what the glasses would cost.

screens.why3: Whether I want a waitlist of deaf and hard-of-hearing people to send a pair to is my own call, made from my own plans.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole decision; the two options are distinct and complete.
screens.why5: It adds a closing line without changing anything I typed, and the respondent's line says "this" without leaking the product name or price.

screens.why1: Picking who asks my questions is the natural last step before the link goes out, and the hint answers my first worry by saying every question is also written on screen with type or tap answers.
screens.why2: Two named voices, a play button and a credit cost are clear on first read, though the hint is long.
screens.why3: I know my people: the hard-of-hearing ones will strain at a voice and the deaf ones will read, so I can judge which voice is clearer.
screens.why4: Two distinct voices with Daphne preselected, but for deaf adults the answer I'd most likely want is missing: a text-only or captions-first option, or an ASL signer.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and the text message link, and nothing about the glasses or captions product leaks to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne (voice + captions) · Saskia (voice + captions) · Text only, no voice

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will answer comes right after choosing who asks them, so as the founder I see why this is asked here, just before sending.
screens.why2: Every option is plain to me, and 'read and tap' is exactly how I would put it for my people.
screens.why3: I know my wearers well: many of them read captions all day, and some speak while others do not, so I can choose from what I know.
screens.why4: The Daphne option is pitched at hearing people ('asks each question aloud', 'Hear her', speech-catch rates in loud rooms) when my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing, and nothing mentions captions-first or signing, though Read and tap does cover the true answer.
screens.why5: It keeps my words, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing about AirCaps or the glasses leaks into what respondents will see.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? — Read and tap (type or tap, no sound needed) / AI interviewer Daphne, every question captioned on screen, answer by typing, tapping or speaking / Let them choose

screens.why1: Choosing who receives the link is the natural last step after deciding how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults will answer, so it is obvious why it is asked here.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass, though 'the Contacts page' names a Keel screen I have not seen yet in this flow.
screens.why3: I know who I will reach first (the people from our TranscribeGlass days, plus HLAA chapters and deaf Facebook groups), so I can answer this from my own work.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and an open group link are complete and distinct for how I would reach this community, and the group option fits deaf community spaces well.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and my pick of people I know by name is offered as typed.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right under the title, but the deciding line "3 holding · 7 people answered" puts a count of cards next to a count of people, so at first I read it as 3 of 7 people holding, not all 3 cards holding.
screens.why_b2: Each card plainly shows what was counted, over 7 people, and the bar at 5 of 7, though "yes or yes, with some steps" is clumsy wording.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are exactly the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what all three holding means for AirCaps or what I should do next; the only extra line explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but 7 of 7 from seven people is never flagged as a small sample, and the solution statement is garbled ("wearing the glasses an app on lightweight glasses shows"), which muddies what was actually tested.
screens.instead: All 3 of your solution beliefs held with 7 people (7 of 7 on each, 3 of them only on a condition): a small but clean read, so look at those 3 conditions before you rely on adoption.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 5 of 7', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts Yes 4, Yes with some steps 3 and No 0 over 7 people, and the strip puts my bar at 5, so all three read at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The title is Compatibility and the line 'their phone was with them and online' is the one I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the phone is not the blocker and sends me to adoption friction, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line still says flatly that the phone 'is not what will stop them' on 7 people, and three of them needed steps.
screens.instead: With 7 of 7 having their phone along and online, the phone looks unlikely to be what stops them, though 7 is a small group. The three who needed steps all asked to try a demo pair first, so check adoption friction below.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said it would have gone better against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 7 people who said 'better', all 'a lot', and the bar marker sits at 5 of 7, so I can read it at once even though the '7 7 a lot · 0 a little' run is a bit cramped.
screens.why_b3: The title is Relative advantage and the belief line is word for word what I checked: following more without asking anyone to repeat.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points me to Adoption friction, but it doesn't say what a unanimous imagined benefit means for my idea or pitch.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 visible, calls it 'a lean, not a call' and flags that the answer is hypothetical, so a 7-of-7 sweep isn't oversold.
screens.instead: All 7 who had a hard conversation say AirCaps would have helped a lot, so the benefit isn't the doubt; it's hypothetical and only 7 people, so the real test is whether they'd wear the glasses paired to the phone (Adoption friction, below).

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answer choices over 7 people, and the bar at 5 of 7, with no more than 1 in 3 against, is marked on the strip, so it reads at a glance.
screens.why_b3: "Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone" is the belief I checked, word for word.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to Harriet, Ruth and Tomás is below, but the only thing below is Tomás's end-seat quote, which says nothing about what would win them over, so I'm left without a concrete next step.
screens.why_b5: The headline 7 of 7 carries '3 on a condition' right beside it, and the count line calls 7 people 'a lean, not a call', so nothing is oversold.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean from 7: 4 would wear them as is and 3 only if clearly worth it, and none said what 'worth it' means, so ask those 3 what would tip them before leaning on the free-returns trial.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on Holding up with 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7 right beside it, and repeats it as 'held, 7 of 7', so I know the verdict and the number behind it.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked: the phone with them and online, and wearing the glasses paired to the phone.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, though the quotes point plainly at one move: let people try a pair on a matinee or a noisy walk before ordering, beyond my 15-day returns.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 is visible, but the screen never says seven people is a small sample; the dangling 'Yes, with some steps for' and the Harriet and Ruth quotes filed under 'steps' for the phone (both about trying the glasses or what it hears) blur what was actually asked.
screens.why_b6: I did not type lens readability under stage lights, picking up audience questions in a big hall, wanting a demo walk while moving, or Tomás's end-seat workaround that makes the glasses only marginal for one-sided loss, and each is a real product or wedge lesson.
screens.instead: Phone and glasses both held 7 of 7 (a small sample of 7); what they added: people want to try a pair in their own hard setting (stage lights, a noisy walk) before buying, a big hall needs the audience mics too, and one-sided loss already has a seat-choice workaround, so offer a try-at-home pair and test hall pickup.

screens.why1: This is the opening screen, and it plainly checks whether I'm the kind of person the study is for before asking anything else.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is exactly how I and other deaf people say it, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: Whether I talk with hearing people each week is my own daily life, so I know the answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and a gate has no escape by the rules.
screens.why5: It drops 'face to face', so texting or video relay with hearing people would also count, which drifts from the founder's in-person conversations, though nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and two options I can hold, though the guidelines' screener form is simply 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Once I've said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost the thread of one this past week before asking me for the story.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd describe what happens when people talk too fast or over noise, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: It happens to me most weeks, at work, in a shop or at dinner, so I know whether it happened in the last seven days.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a yes-or-no gate should have no escape, and here there are two chips, one a full sentence and one "I'd rather not say", which the guidelines say doesn't exist.
screens.why5: It still means a conversation with hearing people that I couldn't follow, and nothing about a product or the founder's labels for me comes through.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's one short question followed by "Yes or no," which is easy to answer by voice.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes · No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I lost track of a conversation with hearing people, showing me a way to follow along is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are words I use every day, so I take it in on one read, though "the app on them" is a slightly odd way to put it.
screens.why3: I know exactly what it costs me to look down at captions or a phone and lose someone's face and lips, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It names the product and says what it does in plain terms, with no internal labels for people like me leaking through.
screens.why6: It is short, plain sentences with no slashes or brackets, easy to hear once, though "read the words" said twice is a little repetitive.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, live captions inside the lens. You wear light glasses, and when people nearby talk, their words show as captions in the lens. The people building it believe you could read along and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: After the card about captions in the lens it makes sense to ask about my phone, but nothing on the card told me the glasses need a phone, so it comes a bit out of nowhere.
screens.why2: "Have your phone with you and online?" is missing its "Did you", so at first it sounds like an instruction, and it asks two things at once: did I have the phone, and did it have signal.
screens.why3: I always know whether my phone was in my bag and had signal at my last conversation, since I lean on it for captions and typing back and forth.
screens.why4: "Yes, with some steps" is odd for having a phone on me; it either was or wasn't, though I suppose it could mean I had to find wifi or turn data on.
screens.why5: The phone-and-online condition comes through, but the dropped "Did you" bends it, and asking about the phone hints at how the product works when the card never said so.
screens.why6: Heard once, "Have your phone with you and online?" sounds like being told to get my phone out rather than being asked, and "yes, with some steps" is a strange thing to hear about a phone.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Did you have your phone on you, with signal? Yes; yes, but I had to sort out the signal; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: It follows the phone question, but it is not clear what 'it' is or why I am asked about steps after saying whether I had my phone online.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but 'it' has nothing clear to point back to, so I would have to read it twice to guess what took steps.
screens.why3: If 'it' means getting my phone ready to help me follow the conversation I could answer, but I would be guessing at what is meant.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the bare 'it' has drifted loose from whatever the founder meant to ask about.
screens.why6: Short and easy to say, but heard once with no anchor the listener cannot tell what 'it' refers to.
screens.instead: Think of that last conversation. What would you have had to do with your phone to have it ready to help you follow along?

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the phone question, asking whether captions in my glasses would have helped that last conversation is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Plain words: would it have made my last conversation go better, a lot, a little, no difference or worse -- I can answer that straight off.
screens.why3: I know how my last conversation went and where I got lost, but I have never worn caption glasses, so how much better it would have been is partly a guess.
screens.why4: The four cover it without overlap, including that it could make things worse (looking at text instead of faces), and I can't tell fits someone who has never tried it.
screens.why5: Only the product's name and the shown idea card reach me, which is on purpose; nothing else of the founder's plan or terms leaks.
screens.why6: One short balanced question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last -- easy to answer on one hearing.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether it would have helped my last conversation, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually wear the glasses to get it.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses paired to my phone is plain to me; I pair my hearing aids and phone all the time.
screens.why3: Whether I'd put glasses on to follow hearing people is something I know about myself from daily life.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided, with a conditional yes but no plain 'probably yes', and it leaves out my real answer: I already wear prescription glasses, so it would depend on getting my lenses in them.
screens.why5: It shows AirCaps on purpose as live captions in glasses, and nothing in the question reads like the company's own jargon about people like me.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options and one escape said last is easy to take in at once.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses paired to your phone. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Only if they fit my own prescription · Probably not · No — chip: I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether I'd wear the glasses, asking what would make it worth it is plausible, but it jumps from wearing them to value without building on my answer about glasses.
screens.why2: Short, everyday words; I can answer it on first read or hearing.
screens.why3: I know what makes a conversation hard to follow, like noise, fast talkers and groups, but saying what would make a product I've never used worth it is partly a guess.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It only names AirCaps from the idea card I was shown, and nothing else of the founder's plan leaks through.
screens.why6: One short question with no list, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would the glasses need to do in a fast or noisy conversation for you to wear them every week?
